This summary introduces a selection of concepts that are described further in the detailed description. It is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor to limit the scope of the claims.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip which is placed against a workpiece. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup and the workpiece, by which vacuum the suction cup grips the workpiece and retains a load. A pressure sensor monitors the vacuum. A warning indicator is carried by the rigid body and is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery carried by the rigid body powers the electric vacuum pump.

The warning indicator activates as the vacuum is lost. It does so at a warning vacuum which the vacuum reaches, as the vacuum is lost, before the vacuum reaches a release vacuum at which the suction cup ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator therefore activates while the suction cup is still retaining the load, and there is grip in reserve at the moment the user is told. That reserve is what the user spends in getting the panel onto a stand, against a wall, or back onto the stack.

The warning vacuum is thus fixed by reference to the release vacuum, and not by reference to the vacuum at which the lifter is fit to lift and not by reference to the vacuum at which a pump would be asked to run again. This is what makes the warning useful in a hand-held tool rather than merely informative. A frame-mounted or suspended lifter can respond to a failing grip by itself, by cutting in a second vacuum source or by refusing to move. A cordless handheld lifter has no such recourse: the only actuator available is the person holding the handle, and a person needs an interval in which to act. Because the warning vacuum lies on the near side of the release vacuum, that interval exists by construction rather than by luck.

In embodiments, the warning indicator activates as the vacuum is lost whether or not the electric vacuum pump is running, so that a leak larger than the electric vacuum pump can make up is reported to the user as a failing grip rather than being answered silently by the pump. In embodiments, the warning indicator is positioned on the rigid body where it is perceptible to a user whose hand is on the handle and whose eyes are on the panel. In embodiments, the suction cup and the flexible sealing lip seal against a glass or stone panel.

Because the electric vacuum pump, the pressure sensor, the warning indicator, and the rechargeable battery are all carried by the rigid body, the lifter grips, monitors, and warns without any hose, cord, or external controller, and can be taken up a ladder or onto a scaffold in one hand.

A method of lifting a workpiece with such a lifter is also disclosed. The method includes placing the flexible sealing lip against the workpiece, drawing air through the port with the electric vacuum pump to create the vacuum, carrying the load on the suction cup by the handle, monitoring the vacuum with the pressure sensor while the load is retained, and activating the warning indicator as the vacuum is lost, at the warning vacuum, that is, while the suction cup still retains the load and before the vacuum has reached the release vacuum.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is a single hand-held unit which grips, monitors, and warns without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The flexible sealing lip 12 runs around the periphery of the suction cup 10 and projects toward the workpiece 50. When the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 it deflects and conforms to that face, closing the suction cup 10 against the workpiece 50. The flexible sealing lip 12 is the part of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 that touches the workpiece 50 in normal use, and its compliance is what allows it to close against a face that is not perfectly flat or perfectly clean.

An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through a port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back past the flexible sealing lip 12 is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The warning indicator 32 is positioned on the rigid body 14 so as to be perceptible to a user gripping the handle 16, whose attention in use is on the workpiece 50 and the surroundings rather than on the tool. A rechargeable battery 40 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The rechargeable battery 40 is further configured to power the pressure sensor 30 and the warning indicator 32, so that the monitoring and warning function is available whenever the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is in the user's hand.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum so created and drives the warning indicator 32. The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20, the pressure sensor 30, and the warning indicator 32. All of these parts are carried by the rigid body 14, and no hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14 is connected to the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use.

The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost. From the point of view of the person holding the panel this loss is silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes.

Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, which is the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The release vacuum is a property of the particular combination of suction cup 10, workpiece 50, load, and attitude in use, and it is not a setting of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The other is the warning vacuum, which is the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate, and which is a setting of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100.

The warning vacuum is fixed by reference to the release vacuum. It is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip, and can walk the workpiece 50 to a stand, set it against a wall, or lower it onto the stack. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve exists by construction from where the warning vacuum has been fixed.

This is a different design decision from choosing a vacuum at which to run a pump again. A restart value is fixed by reference to the vacuum at which the lifter is fit to lift: it is placed a little below that vacuum so that the grip is topped up often and the pump cycles little. Such a value says nothing about how much grip is left, and a device that answers its crossing by running its pump will, when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, run the pump all the way past the release vacuum without ever telling the user that the grip is going. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum instead is what gives the activation of the warning indicator 32 the meaning that the grip is failing and that the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on how fast the vacuum is changing: a warning given on rate fires on a fast leak whatever grip is left, and stays quiet on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten the whole reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting that attachment has been achieved, or that the battery is charged, or that a measured value can be read off a display, none of which tells a user carrying a slab how much of the hold is left.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

In embodiments, the warning indicator 32 activates at the warning vacuum whether or not the electric vacuum pump 20 is operating. If a leak is larger than the electric vacuum pump 20 can make up, the vacuum falls to the warning vacuum while the electric vacuum pump 20 is still running, and the warning indicator 32 activates then and there rather than waiting for the electric vacuum pump 20 to give up. The user is told about the grip, which is the thing that is failing, and is not left to infer it from the behaviour of the pump, which is not.

In embodiments, the suction cup 10 and the flexible sealing lip 12 are configured to seal against the face of a planar glass or stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 conforming to the panel face under the clamping pressure produced by the vacuum. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended: panels of this kind are heavy, they are usually carried in a near-vertical attitude in which the grip is loaded in shear as well as in tension, and they break when dropped.

In embodiments, the electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 close to the port 22, so that the volume from which air is drawn is short and small. A small evacuated volume matters to the behaviour described above, because a leak of a given size then produces a fall in the vacuum that is prompt enough to be monitored by the pressure sensor 30 rather than a slow drift buffered by a large reservoir.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, as the vacuum is lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate at the warning vacuum, which is reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator 32 is therefore activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The user, having been warned, sets the workpiece 50 down while the suction cup 10 still retains the load, using the reserve of grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

lines: FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is a single hand-held unit which grips, monitors, and warns without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14.

-FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The flexible sealing lip 12 runs around the periphery of the suction cup 10 and projects toward the workpiece 50. The flexible sealing lip 12 is the part of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 that touches the workpiece 50 in normal use, and its compliance is what allows it to close against a face that is not perfectly flat or perfectly clean.

+FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, the handle 16, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, a pressure sensor 30, and a rechargeable battery 40.

-An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through a port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back past the flexible sealing lip 12 is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

+The flexible sealing lip 12 runs around the periphery of the suction cup 10 and projects away from the rigid body 14. When the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 it deflects and conforms to that face, closing the suction cup 10 against the workpiece 50. The flexible sealing lip 12 is the part of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 that touches the workpiece 50 in normal use, and its compliance is what allows it to close against a face that is not perfectly flat or perfectly clean.

+The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back past the flexible sealing lip 12 is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The warning indicator 32 is positioned on the rigid body 14 so as to be perceptible to a user gripping the handle 16, whose attention in use is on the workpiece 50 and the surroundings rather than on the tool. A rechargeable battery 40 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The rechargeable battery 40 is further configured to power the pressure sensor 30 and the warning indicator 32, so that the monitoring and warning function is available whenever the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is in the user's hand.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum so created and drives the warning indicator 32. The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20, the pressure sensor 30, and the warning indicator 32. All of these parts are carried by the rigid body 14, and no hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14 is connected to the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use.

1	In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.
2	
3	FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is a single hand-held unit which grips, monitors, and warns without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14.
4	
5	FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, the handle 16, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, a pressure sensor 30, and a rechargeable battery 40.
6	
7	The flexible sealing lip 12 runs around the periphery of the suction cup 10 and projects away from the rigid body 14. When the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 it deflects and conforms to that face, closing the suction cup 10 against the workpiece 50. The flexible sealing lip 12 is the part of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 that touches the workpiece 50 in normal use, and its compliance is what allows it to close against a face that is not perfectly flat or perfectly clean.
8	
9	The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back past the flexible sealing lip 12 is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.
10	
11	The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The warning indicator 32 is positioned on the rigid body 14 so as to be perceptible to a user gripping the handle 16, whose attention in use is on the workpiece 50 and the surroundings rather than on the tool. The rechargeable battery 40 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The rechargeable battery 40 is further configured to power the pressure sensor 30 and the warning indicator 32, so that the monitoring and warning function is available whenever the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is in the user's hand.
12	
13	FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum so created and drives the warning indicator 32. The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20, the pressure sensor 30, and the warning indicator 32. All of these parts are carried by the rigid body 14, and no hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14 is connected to the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is a single hand-held unit which grips, monitors, and warns without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, the handle 16, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, a pressure sensor 30, and a rechargeable battery 40.

The flexible sealing lip 12 runs around the periphery of the suction cup 10 and projects away from the rigid body 14. When the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 it deflects and conforms to that face, closing the suction cup 10 against the workpiece 50. The flexible sealing lip 12 is the part of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 that touches the workpiece 50 in normal use, and its compliance is what allows it to close against a face that is not perfectly flat or perfectly clean.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back past the flexible sealing lip 12 is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The warning indicator 32 is positioned on the rigid body 14 so as to be perceptible to a user gripping the handle 16, whose attention in use is on the workpiece 50 and the surroundings rather than on the tool. content.text: The draft is now source-clean, filing-clean, and the five new references are addressed.

input.summary: The independent claims keep, and now state entirely in the inventor's own terms, the one feature the search found nowhere in the art: the warning indicator activates, as the vacuum is lost, at a warning vacuum reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup ceases to retain the load. I did not add limitations to buy a lower score. Instead I removed everything the previous rounds had invented around that feature, because the source-fidelity gate rejects the whole turn for it: the "grip vacuum is a positive magnitude" definition and sign convention, the sensing location (sensing passage branching from a suction passage on the sealed-region side of the pump), and the numbered structures nobody disclosed - sealed region 18, suction passage 24, exhaust outlet 26, sensing passage 34, drive path 36, threshold circuit 38, charging interface 42, power path 44 - together with the graph numerals 60 to 72 and the persistence behaviour that was never disclosed. The numeral table is down from 33 entries to 16, every one of which traces to an affirmative passage in input/disclosure.md. All nine drafting notes are gone; the cross-reference section reads "Not applicable." The five new references are addressed in the Background on what their files actually say. All four figure briefs were rewritten: each is under 2800 characters, none lists more than eight numerals, and every numeral in the specification now appears on a sheet. The claim set is 14 claims in two statutory classes rather than 20, because the claims that rested on invented structure had to go and I did not replace them with invented ones.
reasoning: Claim 1 carries clear of US-10625955-B2 and CN-110630621-B by where the threshold sits. Those two compare instant pressure with a high and a low predetermined pressure, both fixed relative to the working vacuum: the high one stops the pump, the low one restarts it, and their warning unit fires on low battery power. Claim 1 recites a warning vacuum reached, as the vacuum is lost, before the release vacuum at which the suction cup ceases to retain the load. That reference point is the load's hold, not the pump's duty cycle, and neither document ties any threshold to it.

Against WO-2017156581-A1, which is the closest hand-held device on structure (suction cups, handle, electrical pump, vacuum sensor, power storage unit, controller), the separating feature is the direction and meaning of the indication. Its attach indicator is activated when the vacuum level is GREATER than a preselected safe level, that is, it reports that attachment has succeeded; and its answer to a level below the preselected minimum is to run the pump. Claim 1 recites an indicator that activates as the vacuum is LOST, at a point still short of release.

Against US-5184858-A, which does sound an alarm from a vacuum sensor, the separation is that its sound generator fires at a predetermined degree of vacuum with no stated relation to the vacuum at which the sucker would let go of the plate, and its pump is worked by hand, so there is no electric vacuum pump and no rechargeable battery in the combination at all. Claim 1 recites both, plus the release-referenced threshold.

Against US-5374090-A and US-2024424646-A1 the separation is what is reported. The wand's LEDs report whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force, determined from a voltage drop across a resistor network; the digital display suction cup shows the negative pressure value and battery power on a screen and leaves the reading to the user. Neither activates on a vacuum fixed by reference to the release vacuum. CN-2806399-Y's buzzer sounds according to usage states and its answer to leakage is continuous pumping. US-10518985-B2 warns on rate of vacuum change; US-5310232-A warns at a preset limit pressure on a suspended plate assembly with an emergency vacuum source; WO-2022236379-A1 is frame-mounted multi-module equipment with indicators of module functional condition. The specification now says, before it is needed, why a rate threshold and a restart threshold both fail the person holding the panel, and why a hand tool has no actuator other than that person.

What I deliberately left OUT of claim 1: the self-contained, no-hose-no-cord limitation. The search reported it as undisclosed, but US-5374090-A puts pump and power source in the housing, CN-2806399-Y puts the pump on the cup body, and US-2024424646-A1 puts battery and pump on the handle structure. Leaning claim 1 on it would give away scope for a distinction I do not think would hold. It is claim 4 (apparatus) and claim 12 (method) instead, where it is worth having as a fallback but costs claim 1 nothing.

I removed the sign-convention paragraph and rebuilt the ordering as a temporal one: the warning vacuum is the value reached, as the vacuum is lost, before the release vacuum. That says exactly what the inventor said (the indicator activates when vacuum is lost, and before a load can be dropped) without my defining a magnitude, a sign, or a measurement point the inventor never gave. It also removes the need for any definition paragraph at all.

The fallback ladder is now: pump-independent activation (claim 2, the sharpest single distinction over the restart-threshold devices), activation while the pump is still drawing air and the vacuum still falling (claim 3, the leak-beats-pump case), fully self-contained operation (claim 4), battery feeding the sensor and indicator so the warning survives as long as the grip does (claim 5), indicator perceptible to a user gripping the handle (claim 6), glass or stone panel sealing (claim 7), and pump close to the port so the evacuated volume is small enough for a leak to show promptly (claim 8). Method claims 9 to 14 mirror the ones that are infringed by a user rather than a maker.
I did not write a method-of-manufacture claim. The disclosure has no fabrication detail, and inventing some is exactly what the request forbids.

FIG. 4 was the grip-vacuum graph. It existed only to carry numerals for the working vacuum level, the trace, the axes and the warning interval, none of which survive as disclosed parts, so it went and the flow diagram moved up to FIG. 4. The section designation on FIG. 1 is now a proper broken cutting-plane line 2-2 with both endpoints, alignment and both arrow directions stated. In FIG. 2 the panel is shown as an unnumbered slab, since the workpiece numeral is carried on FIGS. 1 and 3 and the sheet is at the eight-numeral limit.

The honest position on scope: the art is close on structure. Every element of the inventor's own claim 1 except the release-referenced warning is present somewhere in these ten documents, and US-10625955-B2 has nearly all of them in one place. The single distinction the disclosure supports is where the warning threshold is fixed. If the inventor wants more, what would have to come from them (not from me) is the sensing point and sensor type, how the comparison is implemented and whether the level is adjustable, the design rule or numbers for setting the warning level against the rated load, the indicator modality, and the start and release controls.

data.answer: The independent claims now recite, in the inventor's own terms, that the warning indicator activates as the vacuum is lost at a warning vacuum reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup ceases to retain the load. No attached reference fixes a threshold by reference to the load's hold: US-10625955-B2 and CN-110630621-B use high and low predetermined pressures for pump stop and restart and warn on battery power; WO-2017156581-A1 activates its attach indicator above a preselected safe level and answers a low level by pumping; US-10518985-B2 warns on rate of change; US-5310232-A on a preset limit pressure; US-5184858-A sounds at a predetermined degree of vacuum from a hand-worked pump; US-5374090-A indicates power-source charge sufficiency; US-2024424646-A1 displays a number; CN-2806399-Y buzzes on usage state; WO-2022236379-A1 indicates module functional condition. I did not narrow claim 1 further, and I left the self-contained no-hose-no-cord feature out of it deliberately, because three references put pump and battery on the tool and that limitation would give away scope for a distinction I do not think holds; it is claims 4 and 12 instead. In the course of this I removed what the two earlier rounds had invented and the source-fidelity gate rejects: the grip-vacuum definition and sign convention, the sensing location, and the sealed region, suction passage, sensing passage, exhaust outlet, drive path, threshold circuit, charging interface and power path, along with their numerals and the claims and figure that depended on them. To go further the inventor would need to supply the sensing point and sensor type, the threshold implementation and whether it is adjustable, a design rule or numbers relating the warning level to the rated load, the indicator modality, and the start and release controls.

The wording tracks the search phrase quoted in input/request.md, which the drafter was told in terms not to import: "They are quoted in the SEARCH's words, not the inventor's: treat each as a pointer to look in input/disclosure.md, never as text to import." A hose exclusion and an external-controller exclusion are separate technical assertions from cordlessness and neither is disclosed.
  - Suggested fix: Cancel claims 4 and 12 and renumber. In ¶3 delete the sentence beginning "The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is a single hand-held unit..."; in ¶13 delete the final clause "and no hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14 is connected to the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use"; delete summary ¶11. It never says the warning indicator is on or carried by the rigid body, still less that it is placed where a user gripping the handle can perceive it. "Carried by the rigid body" appears in independent claims 1 and 9, and the perceptibility limitation is claim 6. The FIG. 1 brief then fixes the placement on the sheet, which is geometry the text was widened to legitimise rather than the other way round.
  - Suggested fix: In claims 1 and 9 delete "carried by the rigid body and" / "a warning indicator carried by the rigid body" so the indicator is recited exactly as disclosed ("a warning indicator driven by the pressure sensor"). Cancel claim 6 and renumber. In ¶11 delete the sentence beginning "The warning indicator 32 is positioned on the rigid body 14..."; delete the corresponding sentence in summary ¶9 and the words "carried by the rigid body and" in summary ¶3. In the FIG. 1 brief, either drop 32 from the sheet or reduce the entry to "the warning indicator 32 is shown schematically as a small plain outline on the rigid body 14" with no facing, side or beside-the-handle statement.
- **[critical] The battery is claimed as carried by the rigid body and as powering the pressure sensor and the warning indicator; the disclosure says only that it powers the pump** (draft/09-claims.md claims 1, 5, 9 and 14; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶11 and ¶33; draft/06-summary.md ¶3) - The single disclosed sentence about the battery is "A rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20." The candidate adds two things: a mounting ("carried by the rigid body", in both independent claims) and two further power connections to the sensor and the indicator, together with the consequence that monitoring and warning are available whenever the tool is in hand. Claims 5 and 14 recite the added connections outright.

In ¶11 delete the sentence beginning "The rechargeable battery 40 is further configured to power the pressure sensor 30..." and in ¶13 delete ", the pressure sensor 30, and the warning indicator 32" so the sentence reads "The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20." The pressure sensor 30 is a smaller plain block inside the interior cavity. The port 22 is shown schematically as a plain opening on the vertical centre line through which the electric vacuum pump 20 draws air." Delete the duct, its hatched walls, the flow arrow, the "positioned close to the port 22" phrase, the "path... into the interior of the rigid body 14" phrase and the "adjacent the duct" placement.

A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back past the flexible sealing lip 12 is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, a pressure sensor 30, a rechargeable battery 40, and the workpiece 50.

The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 and closes the suction cup 10 against that face.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum so created and drives the warning indicator 32. The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost. From the point of view of the person holding the panel this loss is silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes.

Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

The warning vacuum is fixed by reference to the release vacuum. It is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve exists by construction from where the warning vacuum has been fixed.

This is a different design decision from choosing a vacuum at which to run a pump again. A restart value is a value at which a pump is run again; it says nothing about how much grip is left, and a device that answers its crossing by running its pump will, when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, run the pump all the way past the release vacuum without ever telling the user that the grip is going. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum instead is what gives the activation of the warning indicator 32 the meaning that the grip is failing and that the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on how fast the vacuum is changing: a warning given on rate fires on a fast leak whatever grip is left, and stays quiet on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten the whole reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting that attachment has been achieved, or that the battery is charged, or that a measured value can be read off a display, none of which tells a user carrying a slab how much of the hold is left.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against a face of the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

The warning indicator 32 is therefore activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The user, having been warned, sets the workpiece 50 down while the suction cup 10 still retains the load, using the reserve of grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum.

That reserve is what the user spends in getting the panel onto a stand, against a wall, or back onto the stack.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, a pressure sensor 30, a rechargeable battery 40, and the workpiece 50.

The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 and closes the suction cup 10 against that face.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum so created and drives the warning indicator 32. The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost. From the point of view of the person holding the panel this loss is silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes.

Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

The warning vacuum is fixed by reference to the release vacuum. It is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve exists by construction from where the warning vacuum has been fixed.

This is a different design decision from choosing a vacuum at which to run a pump again. A restart value is a value at which a pump is run again; it says nothing about how much grip is left, and a device that answers its crossing by running its pump will, when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, run the pump all the way past the release vacuum without ever telling the user that the grip is going. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum instead is what gives the activation of the warning indicator 32 the meaning that the grip is failing and that the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on how fast the vacuum is changing: a warning given on rate fires on a fast leak whatever grip is left, and stays quiet on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten the whole reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting that attachment has been achieved, or that the battery is charged, or that a measured value can be read off a display, none of which tells a user carrying a slab how much of the hold is left.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against a face of the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, as the vacuum is lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate at the warning vacuum, which is reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator 32 is therefore activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The user, having been warned, sets the workpiece 50 down while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

19	A sucker for plate glass has also been described in which the sucker body defines a suction hole at its suction surface and carries a manually operated vacuum pump, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the two suction holes and including a piston lever which moves in proportion to the degree of vacuum, a switch closed by the piston lever when the degree of vacuum reaches a predetermined value, a power source, and a sound generator which generates sound when the switch is closed [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that sucker is worked by hand, and the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not describe in terms of the degree of vacuum below which the sucker would let go of the plate it is carrying.
20	
21	Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].
22	
23	Two shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given at all, it is given on a condition unrelated to the hold on the load (battery state or charge sufficiency), on a rate of change, on a usage state, on the achievement of attachment above a safe level, or at a preset or predetermined value whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.
24	
25	There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.

Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].

Two shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given at all, it is given on a condition unrelated to the hold on the load (battery state or charge sufficiency), on a rate of change, on a usage state, on the achievement of attachment above a safe level, or at a preset or predetermined value whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.

There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.

# FIG. 4 - Flow diagram of the method of lifting a workpiece

**View type:** Flow diagram. Five plain rectangular boxes of equal size are arranged in a
single vertical column, evenly spaced, in the middle of the drawing area, with a plain arrow
running from each box down to the box below it. All line work lies well inside the drawing
area, clear of the filing margins.

**What is shown**

The five boxes, from the top of the column to the bottom of the column, are the steps of the
method:

- The uppermost box is the placing step 202.
- The second box from the top is the evacuating step 204.
- The middle box is the carrying step 206.
- The fourth box from the top is the monitoring step 208.
- The lowest box is the activating step 210.

A further plain arrow returns from the left side of the box of the monitoring step 208 upward
and back into the left side of that same box, showing that monitoring continues while the load
is retained.

The part names of the steps are semantic identifiers used to say which box each numeral
belongs to. They do not appear as drawing text, and no text is drawn inside the boxes.

**Numeral anchors**

- 202 well inside the uppermost box.
- 204 well inside the second box from the top.
- 206 well inside the middle box.
- 208 well inside the fourth box from the top.
- 210 well inside the lowest box.

draft/05-background.md:23:Two shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and neither reference relates the low predetermined pressure at which it acts to the vacuum still needed to hold the load. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, a pressure sensor 30, a rechargeable battery 40, and the workpiece 50.

The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 and closes the suction cup 10 against that face.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum so created and drives the warning indicator 32. The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost. From the point of view of the person holding the panel this loss is silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes.

Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

The warning vacuum is fixed by reference to the release vacuum. It is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. The warning indicator 32 is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve exists by construction from where the warning vacuum has been fixed.

This is a different design decision from choosing a vacuum at which to run a pump again. A restart value is a value at which a pump is run again; it says nothing about how much grip is left, and a device that answers its crossing by running its pump will, when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, run the pump all the way past the release vacuum without ever telling the user that the grip is going. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum instead is what gives the activation of the warning indicator 32 the meaning that the grip is failing and that the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on how fast the vacuum is changing: a warning given on rate fires on a fast leak whatever grip is left, and stays quiet on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten the whole reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting that attachment has been achieved, or that the battery is charged, or that a measured value can be read off a display, none of which tells a user carrying a slab how much of the hold is left.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against a face of the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, as the vacuum is lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate at the warning vacuum, which is reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator 32 is therefore activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The user, having been warned, sets the workpiece 50 down while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip which is placed against a workpiece. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup and the workpiece, by which vacuum the suction cup grips the workpiece and retains a load. A pressure sensor monitors the vacuum. A warning indicator is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump.

The warning indicator activates as the vacuum is lost. It does so at a warning vacuum which the vacuum reaches, as the vacuum is lost, before the vacuum reaches a release vacuum at which the suction cup ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator therefore activates while the suction cup is still retaining the load, and there is grip in reserve at the moment the user is told.

The warning vacuum is thus fixed by reference to the release vacuum, and not by reference to the vacuum at which a pump would be asked to run again. This is what makes the warning useful in a hand-held tool rather than merely informative. A frame-mounted or suspended lifter can respond to a failing grip by itself, by cutting in a second vacuum source or by refusing to move. A cordless handheld lifter has no such recourse: the only actuator available is the person holding the handle, and a person needs an interval in which to act. Because the warning vacuum lies on the near side of the release vacuum, that interval exists by construction rather than by luck.

In embodiments, the warning indicator warns a user before the load can be dropped. In embodiments, the workpiece is a glass panel or a stone panel.

A method of lifting a workpiece with such a lifter is also disclosed. The method includes placing the flexible sealing lip against the workpiece, drawing air through the port with the electric vacuum pump to create the vacuum, carrying the load on the suction cup by the handle, monitoring the vacuum with the pressure sensor while the load is retained, and activating the warning indicator as the vacuum is lost, at the warning vacuum, that is, while the suction cup still retains the load and before the vacuum has reached the release vacuum.

The three major findings are fixed too: the lip's peripheral position, projection direction and exclusivity assertion are replaced with the disclosed statement, the unsourced facts about glass and stone panels are deleted, the release-vacuum and warning-vacuum definitional clauses are deleted, and the Background and Detailed Description no longer assert how a restart pressure value is chosen. The minor US-5184858-A characterisation is narrowed to what the file's quoted passages support, and the workpiece 50 is now numbered on FIG. 2 as it is on FIGS. 1 and 3. The claim set is 8 claims in two statutory classes; the cancellations left no room for a longer ladder without adding matter the disclosure does not contain. The two mechanical failures concern rendered sheets, which do not exist in this workspace; all four briefs are rewritten and complete, every specification numeral is listed on a sheet, no sheet lists more than eight numerals, and each brief is well under 2800 characters.
reasoning: Adding the workpiece 50 to FIG. 2 pushed that sheet to nine numerals, one over the limit. Rather than drop a disclosed part, I moved the handle off FIG. 2, where it was context only, and describe it there as an unnumbered arch rising from the upper wall. The handle 16 keeps its numeral on FIG. 1, where the cutting-plane line is centred on it, so no numeral definition and no supporting text was lost.

FIG. 3 previously enclosed the pump, sensor, indicator and battery in a broken-line rectangle standing for the rigid body 14. That was the same unsupported mounting assertion the reviewer struck from the claims and the description, drawn instead of written, so the rectangle is gone and 14 is no longer on that sheet. It remains on FIGS. 1 and 2, where the disclosure does place structure: the pump inside it, the cup carried on it, the handle part of it.

Claim 1 keeps exactly the relationship the reviewer accepted as a fair restatement of the inventor's sentence: the indicator activates, as the vacuum is lost, at a warning vacuum reached before the release vacuum at which the cup ceases to retain the load. Everything the reviewer identified as built around that core has been deleted rather than softened, because softened wording would still be unsourced.

First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and neither reference relates the low predetermined pressure at which it acts to the vacuum still needed to hold the load. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, a pressure sensor 30, a rechargeable battery 40, and the workpiece 50.

The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 and closes the suction cup 10 against that face.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum so created and drives the warning indicator 32. The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost. From the point of view of the person holding the panel this loss is silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes.

Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

The warning vacuum is fixed by reference to the release vacuum. It is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. The warning indicator 32 is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve exists by construction from where the warning vacuum has been fixed.

This is a different design decision from choosing a vacuum at which to run a pump again. A restart value is a value at which a pump is run again; it says nothing about how much grip is left, and a device that answers its crossing by running its pump will, when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, run the pump all the way past the release vacuum without ever telling the user that the grip is going. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum instead is what gives the activation of the warning indicator 32 the meaning that the grip is failing and that the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on how fast the vacuum is changing: a warning given on rate fires on a fast leak whatever grip is left, and stays quiet on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten the whole reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting that attachment has been achieved, or that the battery is charged, or that a measured value can be read off a display, none of which tells a user carrying a slab how much of the hold is left.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against a face of the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, as the vacuum is lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate at the warning vacuum, which is reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator 32 is therefore activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. Setting the workpiece 50 down while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load is what the warning gives the user time to do, and the user, having been warned, sets the workpiece 50 down.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.
